items.prompt: Per this unit, what is "power" in an organizational sense?
choices: Being liked by leadership
The ability to actually get a decision adopted, funded, staffed, and sustained — a real, distinct resource separate from being technically correct
Having the most senior title in the room
Being the loudest or most persistent voice in a meeting
items.explanation: Power is specifically the capability to make things happen — allocate resources, get something prioritized, get a team to change direction. It's explicitly distinguished from being liked, being senior, or being loud, none of which guarantee that capability.
items.reference:
Looks like power

Liked, senior, loud

Is power

Gets things adopted, funded, staffed

Why: power is a capability that moves outcomes, not a personality trait or a title.
items.learnMore:
What power actually is

It's tempting to treat power as a vibe — someone seems important, someone seems confident — but the definition this unit uses is functional, not perceptual.

TraitConfers power?
Being well-likedNot by itself
Seniority/titleOnly if it grants real authority
Speaking loudly/oftenNo
Can allocate budget, headcount, priorityYes

Common mistake

Assuming the most confident or most senior-sounding person in a meeting is automatically the one with power to move a decision — sometimes true, often not.

Popularity is irrelevant to power in every case
Power only comes from formal titles, never from being liked
items.explanation: Popularity can feed one source of power (relationships), but it is not power itself. Power is defined by what it lets you actually accomplish — adoption, funding, staffing — not by how well-liked someone is.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four sources of power described in this unit?
choices: Formal authority (control over budget/headcount/roadmap)
Expertise (a track record that makes your judgment trusted)
Seniority by tenure alone, independent of the other three
Information (context about what decision-makers actually care about)
items.explanation: The four sources named are formal authority, expertise, relationships, and information. Tenure alone isn't listed as a source — someone can accumulate any of the four sources without long tenure, and long tenure with none of the four doesn't by itself confer power in this framework.

items.prompt: Someone says "talking about power at work feels dirty, like I'm admitting to scheming." What does this unit say about that reaction?
choices: The reaction is correct — power is inherently manipulative and shouldn't be discussed openly
Power is a real, neutral resource — not a character flaw in the people who have it — and treating it as inherently dirty just cedes influence to people who aren't squeamish about it
Power should only be discussed by people in formal leadership roles
This reaction only applies to unusually cutthroat workplaces, not typical ones
items.explanation: The unit explicitly frames power as a real resource, not a moral failing, and treats the instinct to avoid discussing it as itself a stance that cedes influence to people who don't share that discomfort — not a virtue in itself.
items.reference:
Treated as dirty

Avoided, seen as scheming

Treated as a resource

Reasoned about deliberately, like any constraint

Why: avoiding the topic doesn't remove power from the equation — it just cedes it to people less squeamish about it.
items.learnMore:
Power as a constraint, not a flaw

Engineers are trained to reason explicitly about constraints — latency budgets, memory limits, deadlines. This unit's core move is treating power the same way: a real variable in the system, not a moral judgment on anyone who has or uses it.

Common mistake

Believing that refusing to engage with power is a neutral, safe choice. It isn't neutral — decisions still get made, just entirely by people who did engage with it.

A power gap — the idea lacked the capability (a sponsor, formal authority, trust, or context) needed to get it adopted, not proof the system itself is dysfunctional
Proof that political skill is beneath serious engineering work
An unusual situation that rarely actually happens in practice
items.explanation: The unit names this exact phrase and reframes it directly: the frustration is real, but the phrase describes a power gap, not a verdict on the organization or a reason to dismiss political skill as unserious.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does "politics" mean in the neutral sense this unit uses the word?
choices: Manipulating people into decisions that don't serve them
The process of getting a group of people with different incentives to align on a decision
Any interaction between an employee and a manager
A specific set of underhanded tactics like credit-stealing or hoarding information
items.explanation: The unit defines politics functionally: aligning people with different incentives toward a shared decision. It explicitly separates this neutral mechanism from its abuses (manipulation, credit-stealing), which are visible instances, not the definition itself.
items.reference:
Politics (neutral sense) — the process of aligning people with different incentives toward a shared decision.

Why: the mechanism itself is neutral; its abuses are what give the word a negative reputation.
items.learnMore:
Mechanism vs. abuse

Every functioning group with more than one stakeholder has to reconcile different incentives somehow. That reconciliation process is what this unit calls politics — it's present whether or not anyone calls it that.

The mechanismAn abuse of it
Aligning different incentives on a decisionCredit-stealing
Finding a sponsor for a good ideaUndermining a colleague
Framing a proposal around real incentivesHoarding information as leverage

Common mistake

Judging the whole mechanism by its worst visible examples — like judging all communication by the existence of lying.

items.prompt: Per L1, what is the actual goal of studying power as a resource in this unit?
choices: To teach manipulation tactics for getting proposals adopted regardless of merit
To make power visible as a factor so it can be reasoned about deliberately, the same way any other constraint on a system would be reasoned about
To convince readers that technical correctness doesn't matter at all
To train readers to avoid ever engaging with anyone who has formal authority
items.explanation: L1 states the goal explicitly: making power a visible, reasoned-about factor, not teaching manipulation. The point is to stop being repeatedly surprised that correctness alone wasn't sufficient, not to bypass merit altogether.
items.reference:
Not the goal

Teaching manipulation

The goal

Make power visible, reason about it on purpose

Why: the unit treats power as a constraint to reason about, the same way you'd reason about latency or budget — not a manipulation toolkit.
items.learnMore:
Why name the goal explicitly

Because "power" and "politics" carry baggage, it's worth being precise about what this unit is and isn't trying to do. It isn't a manipulation playbook — it's a model for why correct ideas sometimes stall, so the response to that stall can be deliberate instead of purely frustrated.

Common mistake

Reading any unit about organizational power as inherently about manipulation. The stated goal here is the opposite: making an existing, unavoidable factor legible.

items.prompt: In L2's model, why is technical correctness described as "necessary but not sufficient" for a proposal's adoption?
choices: Because correctness is actually irrelevant to whether a proposal is adopted
Because correctness gets a proposal to the point of being considered, but adoption also requires reaching someone with the power to act on it and finding it worth their while
Because only formally-authorized proposals can ever be considered
Because incorrect proposals are adopted just as often as correct ones
items.explanation: A correct proposal that never reaches anyone with the power to act, or reaches them but isn't framed around anything they're accountable for, gets shelved — not because it's wrong, but because correctness alone doesn't move the adoption pipeline forward.
items.reference:
Correct
↓ necessary, not sufficient
Reaches power + matched framing → adopted

Why: correctness is the entry ticket, not the whole pipeline.
items.learnMore:
Necessary vs. sufficient

"Necessary but not sufficient" is a precise claim: without correctness, nothing else matters — but with correctness alone, nothing is guaranteed either.

items.prompt: Per L2's adoption pipeline, what has to be true, in addition to finding a sponsor, for a correct proposal to actually get prioritized?
choices: Nothing else — reaching any sponsor is sufficient by itself
The proposal has to be framed in terms of what that specific sponsor is accountable for, not just argued on its own merit
The proposal has to be resubmitted multiple times regardless of the sponsor's response
The sponsor has to personally write the final version of the proposal
items.explanation: L2's pipeline has a second gate after finding a sponsor: the framing has to connect to that sponsor's actual accountability (what they can allocate, or what they're personally measured on) — reaching them alone doesn't guarantee they'll spend their capacity on it.
items.reference:

↓
Reaches a sponsor?
↓
Framed to THEIR accountability?

Why: two separate gates, both required — a sponsor found isn't the same as a sponsor persuaded.
items.learnMore:
Two gates, not one

It's tempting to treat "found a sponsor" as the finish line. L2's pipeline treats it as gate one of two — the second gate (matched framing) is just as often where a good proposal stalls.

GateFailure mode if missed

Match their accountabilitySeen, agreed with, still not prioritized

Common mistake

Assuming a sponsor who agrees the idea is good will therefore act on it. Agreement and prioritization are different things — prioritization requires it to connect to what they're on the hook for.

items.prompt: Per L2, why can a correct-but-unsponsored proposal and a genuinely bad proposal look identical from the outside?
choices: Because they're actually the same thing — a correct proposal that stalls was secretly flawed all along
Because both produce the same visible outcome ("shelved"), even though the underlying cause is completely different — one lacks power behind it, the other lacks merit
Because all proposals in every org get shelved eventually regardless of quality
Because reviewers deliberately hide the real reason a proposal was rejected
items.explanation: L2 makes this explicit: a correct proposal with no sponsor, or with a framing mismatch, produces the exact same outward result (shelved) as a genuinely bad proposal. The cause differs entirely even though the observable outcome doesn't.
items.reference:
Bad proposal

Shelved — correctly, on merit

Good, unsponsored proposal

Shelved — same visible outcome, different cause

Why: the outcome looks identical from outside; the cause is completely different.
items.learnMore:
Same symptom, different diagnosis

This is exactly why "I was right and it didn't matter" is disorienting: the observer (and sometimes the author) can't distinguish the two cases just by looking at the outcome. Distinguishing them requires checking the pipeline directly — was there a sponsor, was the framing matched — not just noting that it stalled.

Common mistake

Concluding "it got shelved, therefore it must not have been good enough." Shelved is consistent with both explanations — check the pipeline, not just the outcome.

items.prompt: If you only know that a proposal got shelved, can you conclude from that fact alone whether it was actually a bad idea?

items.learnMore:

Every time a sponsor backs a proposal, they're spending some of their own standing on it. That's sustainable when it's part of a two-way relationship — helping with the sponsor's own priorities, being reliable — and unsustainable when it's purely extractive.

Common mistake

Assuming a sponsor who backed you once will keep backing you indefinitely regardless of what you do for them in return. Trust compounds — and depletes — like any other resource.
